opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons it really came together this year.

The first is that the base models finally crossed a threshold. For a long time, people talked about agents, but the models simply weren't capable enough. You'd ask them to do a multi-step task, and somewhere around step three or four they'd lose track, make a small error, and then the whole thing would fall apart. Now, with reasoning models, the models can actually think before they act, reflect on their mistakes, and recover. That changes everything for long-horizon tasks.

The second reason, and this is something I care a lot about as someone working on reinforcement learning, is that RL has become a practical tool for training these models. Before, most of the capability came from pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, which is basically imitation. But an agent needs to interact with an environment, try things, fail, and learn from the outcome. That's exactly what RL is for. This year we've seen that if you put a model into a real environment, a browser, a code sandbox, a search engine, and train it end-to-end with RL, it develops behaviors you can't easily get from imitation alone. It learns to search more, to verify, to keep going when it doesn't find the answer immediately.

The third reason is products. Deep Research-style products, coding agents, these are things ordinary users actually pay for and use every day. When people start relying on something for real work, rather than just demos, that's when you know a new era has begun.

But I'd add one caveat. Saying 2025 is the year of agents doesn't mean agents are solved. I'd say it's more like the starting point. Agents today are still quite fragile. They work well on tasks with clear feedback, like coding or information search, but on open-ended tasks with long horizons and fuzzy goals, there's still a big gap. So to me, 2025 is the year agents became real, and the next few years are about making them truly reliable. A lot of that progress, I believe, will come from scaling up RL, better infrastructure, and better environments.

r001.rationale: The response cites models becoming capable enough for long-horizon tasks and RL becoming practical for training agents as reasons the agent era arrived in 2025.

r002.rationale: It discusses RL gains for agents but does not mention multimodal models or exploring analogous gains in them.

r003.rationale: It names browser, coding, and search tools and user-facing products, but does not identify general-purpose interfaces as a direct application of multimodal models.

fable-5.1.text:
I agree with it, but maybe for a slightly different reason than most people. The usual argument is that the models got good enough, and that's true, but I think the more important thing is that the way we train models changed.

For a long time, the dominant paradigm was pretraining plus a bit of supervised fine-tuning, and then RLHF to make the model polite and helpful in a single turn. That produces a very good chatbot. But a chatbot is fundamentally a one-shot thing: you ask, it answers, done. An agent is different. An agent has to take an action, observe what happens, maybe fail, and keep going for ten, twenty, a hundred steps before you know whether it succeeded. That's a multi-step decision problem, and the thing that actually solves multi-step decision problems is reinforcement learning.

What happened around late 2024 and into 2025 is that people figured out how to do RL at scale on top of large language models, with verifiable rewards, on long-horizon tasks. First it showed up in math and reasoning, the o1 and R1 style of work, where the model learns to think longer. But the same machinery transfers almost directly to tool use, to coding, to browsing, to anything where you can check the final outcome. Once you can train a model end to end on "did you finish the task or not," rather than on "does this single response look nice to a human," the model starts to learn things like error recovery, planning, when to retry, when to ask for help. Those are agentic behaviors, and you basically cannot get them from imitation alone.

The second piece is infrastructure. People built environments. Two years ago, if you wanted to train an agent, you'd spend most of your time writing the sandbox, the tool interface, the evaluation. Now there are real benchmarks, SWE-bench and things like it, there's standardization in how tools are exposed, and the engineering of running thousands of rollouts in parallel is mostly solved. That lowers the barrier a lot.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that it started working in production. Coding agents are the clearest example. Developers are actually letting a model open a repo, run tests, fix things, and submit a pull request. That's not a demo anymore. When one domain crosses that line, it tells you the recipe is right and the other domains are just behind by some months.

So when I say 2025 is the year of agents, I don't mean every agent problem is solved. Long-horizon reliability is still hard, generalization outside the training distribution is still hard. What I mean is that this is the year the recipe became clear: a strong base model, plus RL on real tasks with real outcomes, plus scalable environments. Before this year, people were arguing about which direction to go. Now the direction is pretty obvious, and the competition is about who executes it best.

r001.rationale: The response links capable base models with reinforcement learning at scale on real, long-horizon tasks as the recipe that made agents viable in 2025.

r002.rationale: It describes RL gains for reasoning and transfer to tools, coding, and browsing, but does not connect those gains to exploring multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It discusses tool-using agents and coding workflows, but does not identify agents operating general-purpose interfaces as an application of multimodal models.

astra-6.text:
I think the key change is that we’re moving from AI that answers questions to AI that can carry out tasks. An agent needs to understand a goal, decide what to do next, use tools, and adjust when something doesn’t work. Those capabilities are starting to come together.

But I’d distinguish between the year agents become useful and the year they become fully autonomous. A system can be impressive in a demonstration and still need a lot of supervision in everyday work. The real test is whether it can complete a useful task reliably, at a reasonable cost, without someone correcting it at every step.

So that’s how I’d frame 2025: agents becoming practical in specific workflows, with clear boundaries and human oversight. That’s already a meaningful shift.

r001.rationale: The response describes capabilities coming together but does not attribute the agent era to capable foundation models and mature reinforcement-learning methods.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss reinforcement learning on text models or extending those gains to multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It mentions agents using tools, but does not identify multimodal models operating general-purpose interfaces as a user-facing application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think 2025 is the year when we start asking AI to do things, rather than just answer questions. A chatbot can tell you how to solve a problem. An agent can take a goal, use tools, observe what happens, and adjust its next step. That creates the possibility of delegating an actual task.

Several capabilities are coming together: reasoning, coding, and interacting with software. Coding is particularly interesting because an agent can write a program, run it, see an error, and try again. That feedback loop helps it make progress without a person directing every step.

But I would distinguish the year of agents from the year of fully autonomous agents. Reliability is still a challenge, especially over long tasks, where small mistakes can accumulate. I expect useful adoption to begin with bounded tasks where success is clear and people can review consequential actions. So, for me, “the year of agents” means the beginning of practical delegation, with human oversight still playing an important role.

r001.rationale: It cites reasoning, coding, and software interaction as converging capabilities, but does not attribute the agent era to capable foundation models and mature reinforcement-learning methods.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss reinforcement-learning gains in text models or extend that rationale to multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It describes agents interacting with software, but does not identify general-purpose interfaces as a user-facing application of multimodal models.
